spots.name: Palacio del Infantado
spots.label: Palacio del Infantado

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the square, but the palace houses the Museum of Guadalajara, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in Guadalajara, Spain, and faces the Plaza de España (known locally also as Plaza de los Caídos). Its main front looks west across the square.
text.description:
The Palacio del Infantado is a 15th-century palace in Guadalajara, built in the Isabelline style and once the seat of the Dukes of the Infantado. Its main front is the reason to come. The limestone is cut into rows of diamond points, the main doorway sits off-centre, and a gallery of balconies runs along the top. Together they make a bold, repeating pattern that suits a phone camera well. From the square you can take in the whole facade in one frame, with no need to stitch anything together.

The palace has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1914. It was damaged in the Spanish Civil War, and since 1973 it has housed the Museum of Guadalajara.

For the photo, stand in the square directly facing the front. Take one straight-on shot with the doorway roughly central in your frame, then a second where you step slightly to one side so the diamond points show their depth. Turn on gridlines so the vertical edges and the balcony line stay straight. Then move in and photograph the stonework alone: the diamonds on their own make a good close-up. Keep people in the foreground if you want a sense of scale.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza de España in Guadalajara. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de España (directly in front of the main facade, which faces west). A full frontal view of the diamond-pointed limestone facade, with the off-centre main doorway and the gallery of balconies along the top. Directly in front of the main facade, which faces west. From here the whole frontal view is visible: the diamond-pointed limestone, the off-centre doorway and the gallery of balconies along the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. If the square feels too tight to fit the top balconies in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the diamond-pointed stonework and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is reportedly good, when the low western sun lights the stonework (per one blog).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the balcony gallery up with a horizontal line, keeping your phone level so the facade does not lean. Place the doorway off the centre line, as it sits in real life, and let the diamond pattern fill the rest. Then take a second shot at 2x or more of the stonework alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the pale limestone looks washed out against the sky. Keep Live Photos on if you like, in case anyone walks through the frame.

spots.name: Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano
spots.label: Panteón de la Duquesa

text.access_note: Photograph the exterior from the public park or street side, because the pantheon stands inside a school campus. Interior opening hours are seasonal, so check locally if you want to visit inside.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Guadalajara, Spain, next to the Parque de San Roque. The pantheon stands inside a school campus beside the park.
text.description: The Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano is a funerary building in an eclectic style. It was designed by Ricardo Velázquez Bosco for María Diega Desmaissières y Sevillano, Countess of Vega del Pozo, who was known locally as the Duchess of Sevillano. Permission was granted in June 1887 and work finished in 1916, the year she died. The plan is a Greek cross, the walls are Novelda stone, and the dome is covered in purple tiles. That dome is the main reason to bring your phone. The purple-tiled dome is the standout feature, seen across the park. The best-known view is of the entrance with the dome and roofs rising behind it, seen across the Parque de San Roque. There is no need to go inside for this photo. The pantheon stands within a school campus with its own walls, so you shoot from the public park or street side. Start and take a wide shot of the whole building with some park in front of it. Then step in or zoom for the dome and the stonework. Check the line of the roof before you press the shutter, because the building is symmetrical and looks best when the gridlines show it straight. The porch of the nearby Ermita de San Roque may offer another view; check it is still open and unobstructed before relying on it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head to the Parque de San Roque in Guadalajara. From there it is about 3 minutes on foot to the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque de San Roque (entrance side, facing the pantheon's approach from the park). The pantheon's entrance and its glazed dome and roofs seen across the park, the view most sources associate with the building. On the entrance side, facing the approach to the pantheon with the building to the south. From here you see the entrance, the dome and the roofs across the park. The porch of the Ermita de San Roque is another possible vantage point; check it is still open and unobstructed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot of the entrance and dome across the park. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for the tiled dome and stonework. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole building, and keep it level so the edges do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No time is specified for this spot. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and dome than midday.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the entrance on the centre line, with the dome above it. Keep a strip of park in the foreground to give a sense of scale. If the hermitage porch turns out to be accessible, you could use the porch opening as a frame around the pantheon.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the purple dome keeps its colour against a bright sky. Live Photos are not needed here.

spots.alt: Pantheon of the Duchess of Sevillano, Guadalajara: a funerary building in an eclectic style. Photo spot

spots.name: Church of San Ginés
spots.label: Iglesia de San Ginés

text.access_note: The square is open to the public, but the church is a working parish church and its opening hours may vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Guadalajara, on Plaza de Santo Domingo, which is the open square it stands on. Plaza Pablo Iglesias is a nearby square.
text.description:
The Church of San Ginés is a working parish church in Guadalajara, and it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1931, Spain's heritage protection for important buildings. What catches the eye is the front of the church: a single, heavy stone facade with two large buttresses and towers topped by belfries. The main facade faces west. The solid, simple shapes make it an easy subject for a phone, because the whole building reads clearly at a glance.

The best view is from Plaza de Santo Domingo, the square the church stands on. From there you see the building at an angle rather than straight on, which still works well for the buttresses and towers. For the full west-facing front, walk round to the west side of the square, where the open space lets you step back far enough to fit the facade, buttresses and both belfry towers into one frame without tilting the phone upwards too much.

Then walk round to the west side of the square and take another for the full front. Move a few steps left or right so the towers sit symmetrically on either side of the frame. Switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the buttresses up with them, so the building does not seem to lean. If you have time, Plaza Pablo Iglesias can give a quieter angle on the church, though check the framing on the day.

It is a place of worship, so be discreet if people are coming and going, and wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza de Santo Domingo in Guadalajara. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is to set the square as your destination. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo (across the plaza from the main west-facing facade, in front of the church). The full stone facade with its flanking buttresses and belfry-topped towers, framed by the open square. From here the view is an angled one, showing the stonework, buttresses and belfry-topped towers framed by the open square. The main facade faces west, so for the full front, walk round to the west side of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the square is too crowded to step back, and keep the building centred to limit stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for a close shot of a belfry.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky is bright but even, such as a light overcast day or a clear morning, as this tends to show the texture of the stone without harsh shadows. If you plan to go inside or very early or late, check the church's opening times first.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the buttresses with the vertical lines so the towers stand straight. Keep the phone level and hold it at chest height rather than tilting it up, which makes the towers lean inwards. For a quieter angle on the church, try Plaza Pablo Iglesias, though check the framing there on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white.
